strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing practical challenges in embodied AI: learning planning knowledge from scratch while being robust to LLM inaccuracies
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with two environments, multiple baselines, state-of-the-art comparisons, thorough ablations, and knowledge conflict experiments demonstrating robustness
Strong empirical results showing clear improvements over baselines (EGA 0.5+ vs 0.4 for DECKARD) and competitive performance with larger models using smaller 7B LLM
Insightful analysis of LLM limitations (Table 7: only 8% exact accuracy in initial predictions) providing empirical justification for adaptive revision
Excellent reproducibility with extensive appendices, pseudocode, prompts, hyperparameters, and implementation details enabling reproduction
Honest discussion of limitations, controller bottlenecks, failure cases (Redstone), and broader impact considerations
Three well-designed complementary components (ADL, FFOM, DEX) with clear motivations, each addressing specific challenges in robust planning
weaknesses: Limited novelty of individual components: ADL revision-by-analogy is straightforward, FFOM is basic empirical tracking, DEX is frontier exploration with minor modifications from DECKARD; contribution is primarily in combination

Severe generalization concerns: all experiments confined to Minecraft variants with strict DAG dependency assumptions; unclear transferability to domains with probabilistic outcomes, conditional dependencies, or different reward structures
Six hyperparameters (x₀, d₀, c₀, αₛ, αᵢ, K) without sensitivity analysis; no principled justification for values or guidance on setting them for new domains, limiting practical applicability

Significant experimental limitations: environment modified with non-standard ore spawning to make learning feasible, reducing realism; baseline adaptations (ADAM's '8 quantities' assumption) appear arbitrary; cited baselines used different LLMs and settings, complicating fair comparison

Critical bottleneck from controller: acknowledged struggles with spatial exploration; large gap between REPOA* oracle (0.79 SR) and competing oracle methods (0.38-0.45) suggests controller limitations dominate planning quality assessment; Redstone 0% SR unexplained

Incomplete failure analysis: Redstone tasks fail completely, several armor tasks at 0-5% SR; attributed vaguely to 'item name ambiguity' with limited investigation into what dependency errors are most problematic

Hyperparameter choices in RevisionByAnalogy lack principled justification: distinction between C(v)>c₀ and C(v)≤c₀ appears arbitrary; scaling factors αₛ=2 and αᵢ=8 lack derivation; operation invalidity threshold x₀=-2 not empirically justified

No statistical significance testing despite reasonable sample sizes; missing sensitivity analysis on initialization quality (three human-written plans); no computational cost comparison with baselines despite expensive training (58 GPU-days for MineRL)

Technical concerns: Frontier definition requires ALL prerequisites experienced (brittle with incorrect graphs); RevisionByAnalogy could propagate errors through recursive calls; EGA metric may be overly strict (requires exact match rather than partial credit)

Minecraft-specific assumptions limit generality: experienced requirement set determination uses pickaxe tiers and crafting mechanics; strict operations (craft/smelt/mine) don't reflect probabilistic or conditional dependencies in other domains

strengths: Well-motivated problem of handling inaccurate LLM knowledge in open-world planning
Comprehensive experimental framework with multiple baselines, ablations, and robustness tests (modified environments)
Clear improvements on dependency learning metrics (Figure 1: REPOA EGA >0.5 vs. DECKARD ~0.4)
Interpretable failure recovery with 'Aha moments' showing knowledge conflict adaptation
Thorough documentation enabling reproducibility (detailed hyperparameters, prompts, plans)
Ablation studies confirm complementary roles of all three components (ADL, FFOM, DEX)
weaknesses: Limited novelty: ADL's RevisionByAnalogy, FFOM's failure counting, and DEX's greedy selection are straightforward heuristics lacking algorithmic innovation; very similar to DECKARD with incremental modifications
Severely restricted scope to Minecraft only (two variants); no evaluation on other open-world domains; unclear generalizability beyond discrete hierarchical dependencies

Critical confounding: STEVE-1 controller struggles with spatial exploration (authors acknowledge), making it impossible to isolate planning robustness from controller limitations; complete Redstone failure (0.00 SR) likely controller-limited

Unfair baseline comparisons: REPOA✱ achieves 0.79 vs. Optimus oracles 0.43-0.45 (Table 1) due to fundamentally different planning paradigms (step-by-step vs. full-plan generation), not dependency learning; different LLM models (GPT-4v vs. Qwen 7B) confound results
Weak long-horizon task performance: 0.54 overall SR (learned) with 0.79 gap to oracle; categorical failures (Armor 0.28, Redstone 0.00) indicate major unresolved limitations

Heavy heuristic design with insufficient sensitivity analysis: Many hyperparameters (x₀, d₀, c₀, αₛ, αᵢ, K) lack justification or ablation; RevisionByAnalogy logic (all resources when C(v)>c₀, analogy otherwise) is ad-hoc without principled grounding
Inconsistent 'from-scratch' claim: requires three human-written plans for initialization; no ablation on effect of initialization errors; contradicts autonomy narrative
Missing critical analyses: No computational cost comparison, hyperparameter sensitivity studies, systematic failure mode analysis beyond one baseline, or investigation of Redstone complete failure
Modified experiment scope too limited: Only two artificial perturbations in one environment; 'Aha moments' anecdotal; unclear if findings generalize to real-world knowledge conflicts
Presentation issues: Critical details relegated to 12 appendices; Algorithm 1 undefined procedure calls; statistical results lack hypothesis testing despite shown variance

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing real limitations in existing LLM-based planning approaches that rely on inaccurate knowledge, fine-tuning, or unrealistic assumptions

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across two Minecraft environments with multiple complementary metrics (EGA for dependency learning, SR for task solving), systematic ablation studies, and knowledge conflict experiments

Strong empirical results showing superior dependency learning curves compared to baselines (EGA >0.5 vs DECKARD ~0.4) and impressive performance on challenging late-game tasks (Gold 0.74, Diamond 0.64) using only a small 7B LLM

Technically sound approach with clear design principles: RevisionByAnalogy uses semantic similarity for plausible corrections, FFOM empirically validates operation choices, DEX enables principled exploration
Excellent reproducibility with complete algorithms, detailed prompts, hyperparameter justifications, and implementation details across extensive appendices
Demonstrates practical accessibility by achieving strong results with minimal resources (7B open-weight LLM, three human-written plans) rather than expensive proprietary models
weaknesses: Limited generalization: Evaluation restricted to Minecraft variants with strict DAG dependencies; unclear how RevisionByAnalogy and semantic similarity-based revision would work in other domains without hierarchical item structures or different naming conventions

Overstated 'from scratch' claim: Requires three human-written plans for bootstrapping; lacks ablation on sensitivity to initial knowledge quality/quantity and no analysis of degraded initialization scenarios

Heavy dependence on controller quality: Performance constrained by STEVE-1 limitations (acknowledged but unaddressed); complete failure on Redstone tasks (0.00 SR) with insufficient root-cause analysis; some items across other groups also fail completely

Incomplete baseline comparisons: DEPS, Jarvis-1, Optimus-1/2 results cited from other papers with different experimental settings; only Optimus-1† reimplemented with same LLM; ore spawn modifications (Appendix H.2.5) are significant environmental changes—unclear if baselines benefit equally

Hyperparameter selection and sensitivity underexplored: Six hyperparameters introduced with vague justification ('balance robustness and efficiency'); no systematic sensitivity analysis; limited guidance for applying to new domains

Incremental component-level novelty: Individual techniques (semantic similarity, success/failure tracking, frontier-based exploration) are relatively standard; RevisionByAnalogy sensible but somewhat ad-hoc lacking formal justification; no theoretical analysis of convergence or failure modes

Statistical reporting gaps: Main results table lacks error bars or confidence intervals; unclear number of random seeds for key experiments; MC-TextWorld shows standard deviation but other results don't

Incomplete failure analysis: Redstone domain failures attributed to 'item name ambiguity' without deep investigation; missing ablations on K and similarity metrics; CRe component somewhat orthogonal to main contribution
